questions.stem: This diagram shows blood crossing the labeled interatrial communication from the right atrium into the left atrium. This defect allows a venous thrombus to reach the systemic circulation, a phenomenon known as what?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pulmonary embolism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fat embolism syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Septic embolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Amniotic fluid embolism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Paradoxical embolism

explanation.summary: A right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale lets a venous embolus bypass the pulmonary filter and enter the systemic arterial circulation (paradoxical embolism), a potential cause of cryptogenic stroke.
explanation.whyCorrect: A right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale lets a venous embolus bypass the pulmonary filter and enter the systemic arterial circulation (paradoxical embolism), a potential cause of cryptogenic stroke.

questions.stem: These paired graphs plot passive, active, and total tension against muscle length, with tension rising then plateauing at greater lengths. Which fundamental muscle property do they illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The force-frequency (Bowditch) relationship

choices.label: B
choices.text: The length-tension relationship

choices.label: C
choices.text: The force-velocity relationship

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ventricular pressure-volume loop

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cardiac function (Frank-Starling) curve

explanation.summary: Total tension equals passive plus active tension; active tension peaks at the optimal degree of actin-myosin overlap, defining the length-tension relationship that underlies preload effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: Total tension equals passive plus active tension; active tension peaks at the optimal degree of actin-myosin overlap, defining the length-tension relationship that underlies preload effects.

questions.stem: This diagram contrasts a normal channel that secretes ions across the membrane with a misfolded 'mutant' channel that fails to reach the surface, resulting in thick overlying mucus. What is the direct consequence of the mutant channel shown?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Overproduction of surfactant by type II pneumocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impaired chloride secretion causing thick, dehydrated mucus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased water secretion that thins the mucus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Excessive sodium secretion into the airway lumen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Impaired oxygen diffusion across the alveolar membrane

explanation.summary: Defective CFTR (cystic fibrosis) reduces apical chloride (and secondarily water) secretion, dehydrating airway surface liquid and producing viscous mucus that impairs clearance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Defective CFTR (cystic fibrosis) reduces apical chloride (and secondarily water) secretion, dehydrating airway surface liquid and producing viscous mucus that impairs clearance.

questions.stem: This figure links clinical conditions to four mechanisms of fluid leak across a capillary bed. The balance of pressures governing this net fluid movement is collectively known as what?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Fick principle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Starling forces

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Frank-Starling mechanism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Laplace's law

choices.label: E
choices.text: Poiseuille's law

explanation.summary: Capillary and interstitial hydrostatic and oncotic pressures (Starling forces) determine net filtration; imbalance (low oncotic pressure, high hydrostatic pressure, increased permeability) or lymphatic obstruction produces edema.
explanation.whyCorrect: Capillary and interstitial hydrostatic and oncotic pressures (Starling forces) determine net filtration; imbalance (low oncotic pressure, high hydrostatic pressure, increased permeability) or lymphatic obstruction produces edema.

questions.stem: The left panel shows the diaphragm contracting downward with the chest wall expanding, generating an intrapleural pressure of -4 cm H2O. By what mechanism does this drive air into the lungs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreasing lung compliance so the alveoli recoil open

choices.label: B
choices.text: Actively pumping air in via ciliary action of the airways

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enlarging the thoracic cavity lowers intrapulmonary pressure below atmospheric, so air flows in down the pressure gradient (Boyle's law)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increasing airway resistance to trap incoming air

choices.label: E
choices.text: Raising intrapulmonary pressure above atmospheric, pushing air outward

explanation.summary: During inspiration the diaphragm and chest wall increase thoracic volume; by Boyle's law the pressure falls (alveolar pressure becomes subatmospheric, intrapleural ~ -4 to -7 cm H2O), and air flows in until pressures equalize. Expiration reverses this as the diaphragm relaxes and elastic recoil raises pressure.
explanation.whyCorrect: During inspiration the diaphragm and chest wall increase thoracic volume; by Boyle's law the pressure falls (alveolar pressure becomes subatmospheric, intrapleural ~ -4 to -7 cm H2O), and air flows in until pressures equalize. Expiration reverses this as the diaphragm relaxes and elastic recoil raises pressure.

questions.stem: This diagram labels the muscles involved in breathing. The diaphragm together with the external intercostals are primarily responsible for which action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Valsalva straining only

choices.label: B
choices.text: Swallowing and airway protection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Forced expiration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Quiet (normal resting) inspiration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Quiet passive expiration

explanation.summary: The diaphragm is the chief muscle of quiet inspiration, assisted by the external intercostals; scalenes and sternocleidomastoid are accessory inspiratory muscles for forced breathing. Quiet expiration is passive, while the abdominal muscles and internal intercostals drive forced expiration.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diaphragm is the chief muscle of quiet inspiration, assisted by the external intercostals; scalenes and sternocleidomastoid are accessory inspiratory muscles for forced breathing. Quiet expiration is passive, while the abdominal muscles and internal intercostals drive forced expiration.

questions.stem: In this plot of left ventricular pressure and volume across the cardiac cycle, during the phase labeled isovolumetric ventricular contraction the pressure rises steeply while the volume stays flat. Why does volume remain unchanged during this phase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All four cardiac valves are closed, so no blood enters or leaves the ventricle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blood is regurgitating backward across the aortic valve

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mitral valve is still open allowing continued filling

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ventricle is relaxing rather than contracting

choices.label: E
choices.text: The aortic valve is open but flow is negligible

explanation.summary: Isovolumetric contraction begins when the mitral valve closes but before the aortic valve opens; with all valves shut, ventricular volume is fixed while tension development rapidly raises pressure. The aortic valve opens only once LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure, starting ejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Isovolumetric contraction begins when the mitral valve closes but before the aortic valve opens; with all valves shut, ventricular volume is fixed while tension development rapidly raises pressure. The aortic valve opens only once LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure, starting ejection.

questions.stem: This graph plots ventilation, perfusion, and the V/Q ratio from the base to the apex of an upright lung. Why does the V/Q ratio rise to its highest value at the apex?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both ventilation and perfusion are highest at the apex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ventilation increases far more than perfusion toward the apex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perfusion falls more steeply than ventilation from base to apex, so blood flow drops relatively more

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ventilation ceases entirely at the apex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Perfusion exceeds ventilation at the apex

explanation.summary: Gravity makes both ventilation and perfusion greatest at the base, but perfusion decreases much more sharply toward the apex than ventilation does. Because blood flow falls relatively more, the V/Q ratio is high (>1, more ventilation per perfusion) at the apex and low (<1) at the base.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gravity makes both ventilation and perfusion greatest at the base, but perfusion decreases much more sharply toward the apex than ventilation does. Because blood flow falls relatively more, the V/Q ratio is high (>1, more ventilation per perfusion) at the apex and low (<1) at the base.
